differential.name: Obstructive biliary disease (choledocholithiasis or biliary stricture)

supporting_evidence.finding: Total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL (severe hyperbilirubinemia)
Normal ALT (12.6 U/L) with cholestatic pattern
INR 2.5 (coagulopathy)
Platelet count 102 ×10³/µL (mild thrombocytopenia)
Age 75, male, obesity (BMI ≥ 30) – risk factors for gallstones
Metabolic syndrome components (HTN, pre‑diabetes, dyslipidemia)

differential.reasoning: Severe direct hyperbilirubinemia with normal transaminases in an elderly obese male strongly points to extra‑hepatic biliary obstruction. The coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia can be secondary to cholestasis‑related vitamin K malabsorption. This is the most common cause of this laboratory constellation in this age group.

differential.name: COVID‑associated cholangiopathy

supporting_evidence.finding: Severe COVID‑19 infection in 2020 with pneumonia and AKI
Marked hyperbilirubinemia with normal ALT
Elevated ferritin (631.9 µg/L) and CRP (11.7 mg/L) – persistent inflammatory state
Prior COVID‑related DVT and systemic inflammation

differential.reasoning: COVID‑19 can cause a cholangiopathic picture months after infection, especially in patients who had severe disease and renal injury. The cholestatic labs without hepatocellular injury fit this entity, making it a plausible secondary diagnosis.

differential.name: Cardiac (congestive) hepatopathy

supporting_evidence.finding: History of NSTEMI (2019) and chronic heart‑failure risk factors
Hyperbilirubinemia with normal ALT, mild coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia
Full‑time employment at age 75 suggests compensated but possibly volume‑overloaded state
Elevated LDH (327.5 U/L) – nonspecific but can rise with hepatic congestion

differential.reasoning: Chronic right‑sided congestion from post‑MI heart disease can cause cholestasis, elevated bilirubin, and a mild coagulopathy. This mechanism explains the lab pattern without requiring primary liver injury.

differential.name: Drug‑induced cholestasis / hepatotoxicity

supporting_evidence.finding: Chronic acetaminophen/codeine use (300 mg/15 mg tablets)
High‑intensity atorvastatin 40 mg daily
Prasugrel 10 mg daily – rare reports of immune‑mediated liver injury
Cholestatic labs (high bilirubin, normal ALT)

differential.reasoning: Therapeutic acetaminophen is usually safe, but in the setting of ESRD and possible accumulation, cholestatic injury can occur. Statins and prasugrel are less common culprits but must be considered, especially if imaging is negative.

differential.name: Thrombotic micro‑angiopathy (atypical HUS / TTP)

supporting_evidence.finding: Platelet count 102 ×10³/µL (thrombocytopenia)
LDH 327.5 U/L (elevated)
Prior acute DVT (2020) – suggests a pro‑thrombotic tendency
Leukopenia (3.1 ×10³/µL) – possible marrow stress

differential.reasoning: The combination of thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and a prior thrombotic event raises concern for TMA. Absence of schistocytes or ADAMTS‑13 data keeps probability moderate; urgent testing is warranted because treatment is time‑sensitive.

differential.name: Vitamin K deficiency secondary to cholestasis/malabsorption

supporting_evidence.finding: INR 2.5 with preserved synthetic function (albumin 5.1 g/dL)
Hyperbilirubinemia suggesting cholestasis → impaired fat‑soluble vitamin absorption
Chronic acetaminophen/codeine use – may affect gut flora and vitamin K synthesis

differential.reasoning: A prolonged INR in the setting of normal albumin points toward a functional vitamin K deficiency, often seen with cholestasis. Correctable with vitamin K administration and will help differentiate from intrinsic liver failure.

differential.name: Occult biliary/pancreatic malignancy (cholangiocarcinoma or pancreatic head adenocarcinoma)

supporting_evidence.finding: Marked hyperbilirubinemia with normal ALT
Elevated ferritin and LDH – nonspecific but can be raised in malignancy
Weight loss not documented (absence of data) – a gap that raises suspicion

differential.reasoning: Although less common, obstructive jaundice can be caused by a mass lesion. Imaging will rule this out; the low probability reflects the rarity but high consequence.

differential.name: Long‑COVID systemic inflammatory state

supporting_evidence.finding: Severe COVID‑19 infection in 2020 with lingering fatigue and joint pain
Elevated CRP (11.7 mg/L) and ferritin (631.9 µg/L)
Borderline procalcitonin 0.1 ng/mL

differential.reasoning: Persistent low‑grade inflammation after COVID‑19 can contribute to abnormal acute‑phase reactants but does not directly explain cholestasis. It remains a background contributor.

primary_diagnosis: Obstructive biliary disease (choledocholithiasis or biliary stricture)
clinical_reasoning_summary: The patient is a 75‑year‑old male with extensive cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities and ESRD. The acute laboratory picture is dominated by severe hyperbilirubinemia, a prolonged INR, and mild thrombocytopenia. A cholestatic pattern (high bilirubin, normal ALT) together with age, obesity, and metabolic syndrome makes extra‑hepatic biliary obstruction the most likely cause. COVID‑associated cholangiopathy and cardiac hepatopathy are plausible secondary explanations given the prior severe COVID‑19 infection and known post‑MI heart disease. Drug‑induced cholestasis, TMA, vitamin K deficiency, occult malignancy, and long‑COVID inflammation are retained in the differential with lower probabilities, each supported by specific findings. CKD stage 5 is treated as a background modifier rather than a primary diagnosis for the current abnormalities.
unresolved_findings: Elevated serum albumin (5.1 g/dL) – atypical in liver disease
Borderline procalcitonin (0.1 ng/mL) without clear infection
Psychosocial stress and criminal record – may affect adherence but no direct physiologic link
recommended_workup: Right‑upper‑quadrant (RUQ) abdominal ultrasound with Doppler to assess biliary dilation and hepatic venous flow
Serum bilirubin fractionation (direct vs indirect) to differentiate cholestasis from hemolysis
Peripheral blood smear, haptoglobin, reticulocyte count to evaluate for micro‑angiopathic hemolysis
Trial cessation of acetaminophen/codeine and high‑dose atorvastatin for 48‑72 h, then repeat liver panel
IV vitamin K 10 mg challenge with repeat INR in 6‑12 h
If ultrasound is negative for obstruction, obtain MRCP or contrast‑enhanced CT abdomen for detailed biliary and pancreatic imaging
ADAMTS‑13 activity and complement panel if TMA remains a concern
Serum tumor markers (CA 19‑9, CEA) and, if indicated, endoscopic ultrasound for occult malignancy
Repeat CRP, ferritin, and LDP trends to monitor systemic inflammation
